title: Anthropic shares end first day of trading at $97 as Wall Street closes sharply lower – as it happened
byline: Graeme Wearden, Lucy Campbell, Nadeem Badshah, Nils Pratley, Johana Bhuiyan, Lex McMenamin, Lauren Almeida, Kalyeena Makortoff
excerpt: All ⁠three major US stock indexes ⁠ended the session ​sharply lower after record-breaking IPO by maker behind AI agent Claude

Summary

  • Anthropic shares closed about 17% higher on their first day of trading on Thursday, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety over the technology. The shares ended the session at around $97, up from a record-breaking IPO price of $83, after opening at $111.50 and briefly valuing the creator of the Claude chatbot at about $2tn – making the AI giant’s debut the biggest in history. The company’s valuation after the close stands at around $1.3tn, down from the high of $2tn recorded earlier.

  • However, a 2% slump at the close suggests that Anthropic’s stellar debut wasn’t enough to carry the wider market, which struggled for much of the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 2.2%, while the S&P 500 fell 2% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.3%, preliminary data showed. The S&P 500 fell for a sixth straight day - its longest losing streak since 19 April 2024 – amid concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom and after the drama surrounding Nvidia following the fall of its CEO Jensen Huang last week dragged the company’s shares down.

  • Shortly before ringing the Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued a warning about the dangers of AI but said they weren’t inevitable. “We’ve always been honest that this techology has very real risks … from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems,” he said. “Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people making AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety.”

  • The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders have now reached a total of more than $180bn. We have profiled them here.

  • Anthropic’s listing will serve as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry – in particular, OpenAI, the parent company of ChatGPT – will be watching closely how it fares on the public market as time goes on.

Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse.

Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:

This technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value.

Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this: No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout.

The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight.

Schiff goes on to remind the reader: “We have seen this movie before.” Invoking the bank bailout of 2008, he writes: “If these enormous bets fail, Big Tech and Wall Street billionaires will no doubt turn to Washington for emergency rescue, a path unfortunately well-trodden by corporate giants before them. But the risk should be borne by these companies and their investors, not working families.”

The billionaire investors may be taking this gamble with the assumption that as in 2008, they will be bailed out for failed investments and corporate risk-taking. Congressional majorities should be clear: We won’t bail them out.

Anthropic has made a blockbuster stock market debut – shattering already high expectations.

The AP has put together some numbers to help you understand Thursday’s IPO:

  • The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: $81bn. That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of Thursday’s trading, it offered 980m shares priced at $83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about $75bn in June.

  • Anthropic’s initial valuation: $1.5tn.The initial price per share was set at $83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at $111.50 a share — pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to $2.01tn just before noon ET.

  • By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at $97.17 per share. That’s still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly $1.75tn. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of $2.1tn. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to $1.95tn.

  • Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S+P 500: 11

  • Apple currently leads the pack at $5.1tn, followed by Microsoft ($3.8tn) and Nvidia ($3.6tn), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S+P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over $1tn. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018 .

  • There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If $1tn was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost $122.

Wall Street closes sharply lower as Anthropic's debut fails to revive AI enthusiasm

It’s just gone 4pm ET, which means trading in New York has closed for the day. US stocks slumped at the close, after Anthropic’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalize faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early soar in its share price ebbed.

All ⁠three major US stock indexes ⁠ended the session ​sharply lower, with the benchmark S+P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.

According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46.

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO was priced late on Wednesday at $83 per share, and the stock opened at $111.50 shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation ⁠briefly surpassed $2tn, its momentum began to lose steam.

Most chipmakers were lower, ‌including Micron and Broadcom, among others. And Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.

The Wall Street investment bankers that worked on Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering are set to be awarded a record $550m in underwriting fees, according to the official filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

That is more than they made on SpaceX, which set the previous record at $500m.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley will earn the biggest cut, taking over $200m between them.

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Dan Milmo and Aisha Down

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations.

The opening price of $111.50 per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to around $150bn at the current share price.

Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include the Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher and Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.

Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market, though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.

Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes which it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI.

Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist.

In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”.

Richard Partington and Kalyeena Makortoff

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”

Lisa Bonos in San Francisco

Sameer Shariff, co-founder and CEO of English language education company Cambly, noticed a buzz of energy among Anthropic employees as they were leaving the company’s headquarters in San Francisco yesterday.

Over the past two years, a few employees have left his company to join Anthropic. He’s been thinking about them today.

“I’m happy for them. It’s a big day for the market and for AI,” Shariff said, while chatting with a friend at Joe and the Juice in downtown San Francisco on Thursday. So far, “Anthropic has been funded by all these investors with the inside scoop. But this is a test of how Wall Street responds … all of a sudden the general public has access to participate.”

Shariff said he’s curious how the next six to 12 months will go. “I’m a big fan,” he added.

As we await the close of market valuation of Anthropic at the end of its first day on the market, Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at US-based Walser Wealth Management, wrote: “Anthropic’s IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment, which has been depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks.”

Walser added: “It’s possible that Anthropic could see volatility and downside moves during the Jensen Huang Senate testimony after Thanksgiving, because that is likely to reignite AI fears.

“But if that happens, it could be a good entry point for investors who want to buy Anthropic.”

Lisa Bonos in San Francisco

On a drizzly morning in downtown San Francisco after a massive storm the day before, the mood was sleepy in the Andytown coffee shop atop Salesforce Tower Park. When asked about Anthropic’s IPO today, one barista said “What’s that?” — a clue that not everyone in this tech hub is obsessed with AI.

Anthropic workers do frequent the coffee shop, but they hadn’t seen any today, her colleague said. One patron, smiled when asked if he worked at the maker of Claude. “No, but I wish I did,” he said.

Out on the street, foot traffic seemed lighter than normal, likely due to the weather. But still some tech workers trickled into their offices at 9:30 a.m.

“I wish I was in that building,” a Meta worker, who declined to give his name, said entering his downtown San Francisco office and gesturing to one of Anthropic’s offices across the street. His friends who work at Anthropic have “big plans for what to do with their newfound wads of cash,” he said. “Some people are planning to backpack Asia,” he said. But mostly, they plan to keep working and liquidate slowly, he added.

She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”Read the full report here:Lisa Bonos in San FranciscoSameer Shariff, co-founder and CEO of English language education company Cambly, noticed a buzz of energy among Anthropic employees as they were leaving the company’s headquarters in San Francisco yesterday.Over the past two years, a few employees have left his company to join Anthropic. He’s been thinking about them today.“I’m happy for them. It’s a big day for the market and for AI,” Shariff said, while chatting with a friend at Joe and the Juice in downtown San Francisco on Thursday. So far, “Anthropic has been funded by all these investors with the inside scoop. But this is a test of how Wall Street responds … all of a sudden the general public has access to participate.”Shariff said he’s curious how the next six to 12 months will go. “I’m a big fan,” he added.As we await the close of market valuation of Anthropic at the end of its first day on the market, Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at US-based Walser Wealth Management, wrote: “Anthropic’s IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment, which has been depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks.”Walser added: “It’s possible that Anthropic could see volatility and downside moves during the Jensen Huang Senate testimony after Thanksgiving, because that is likely to reignite AI fears.“But if that happens, it could be a good entry point for investors who want to buy Anthropic.”Lisa Bonos in San FranciscoOn a drizzly morning in downtown San Francisco after a massive storm the day before, the mood was sleepy in the Andytown coffee shop atop Salesforce Tower Park. When asked about Anthropic’s IPO today, one barista said “What’s that?” — a clue that not everyone in this tech hub is obsessed with AI.Anthropic workers do frequent the coffee shop, but they hadn’t seen any today, her colleague said. One patron, smiled when asked if he worked at the maker of Claude. “No, but I wish I did,” he said. Out on the street, foot traffic seemed lighter than normal, likely due to the weather. But still some tech workers trickled into their offices at 9:30 a.m.“I wish I was in that building,” a Meta worker, who declined to give his name, said entering his downtown San Francisco office and gesturing to one of Anthropic’s offices across the street. His friends who work at Anthropic have “big plans for what to do with their newfound wads of cash,” he said. “Some people are planning to backpack Asia,” he said. But mostly, they plan to keep working and liquidate slowly, he added.

blocks.html_en: Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse.

blocks.html_en: Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:

sentences.en: Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:

blocks.html_en:
This technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value.

Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this: No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout.

The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight.

Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse.

Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:

double quotation markThis technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value. Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this: No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout. The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight.

Schiff goes on to remind the reader: “We have seen this movie before.” Invoking the bank bailout of 2008, he writes: “If these enormous bets fail, Big Tech and Wall Street billionaires will no doubt turn to Washington for emergency rescue, a path unfortunately well-trodden by corporate giants before them. But the risk should be borne by these companies and their investors, not working families.”

double quotation markThe billionaire investors may be taking this gamble with the assumption that as in 2008, they will be bailed out for failed investments and corporate risk-taking. Congressional majorities should be clear: We won’t bail them out.

Anthropic has made a blockbuster stock market debut – shattering already high expectations.

The AP has put together some numbers to help you understand Thursday’s IPO:

  • The amount in proceeds raised by the offering: $81bn. That makes Anthropic’s debut the biggest ever. Ahead of Thursday’s trading, it offered 980m shares priced at $83 each, putting Anthropic ahead of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which set a previous record with its IPO proceeds of about $75bn in June.
  • Anthropic’s initial valuation: $1.5tn.The initial price per share was set at $83. But that spiked more than 30% to open at $111.50 a share — pushing the company’s total valuation by half a trillion dollars to $2.01tn just before noon ET.
  • By market close Thursday, Anthropic finished its first trading day at $97.17 per share. That’s still over 17% higher than its initial public offering price, and amounts to a market value of roughly $1.75tn. In June, SpaceX ended its first day of trading on the public market with a valuation of $2.1tn. Its market cap has since fallen to closer to $1.95tn.
  • Number of public companies that have reached the trillion-dollar club in the S+P 500: 11
  • Apple currently leads the pack at $5.1tn, followed by Microsoft ($3.8tn) and Nvidia ($3.6tn), among others. That does not count SpaceX and Anthropic, which also have joined the trillion-dollar club even though they aren’t in the S+P 500 index yet. Only in recent memory have major corporations been valued over $1tn. iPhone maker Apple was the first to pass that threshold, back in 2018 .
  • There are more than 8.2 billion people living on Earth today, per the US Census Bureau. If $1tn was divided among the entire population, each person would receive almost $122.

Wall Street closes sharply lower as Anthropic's debut fails to revive AI enthusiasm

It’s just gone 4pm ET, which means trading in New York has closed for the day. US stocks slumped at the close, after Anthropic’s super-sized IPO failed to revitalize faded enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, as an early soar in its share price ebbed.

All ⁠three major US stock indexes ⁠ended the session ​sharply lower, with the benchmark S+P 500 logging its fifth straight session of losses.

According to preliminary data, the S+P 500 lost 148.39 points, or 2.03%, to end at 7,175.24 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 544.00 points, or 2.23%, to 23,885.88. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,102.71 points, or 2.20%, to 49,095.46.

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO was priced late on Wednesday at $83 per share, and the stock opened at $111.50 shortly before noon. After the company’s market valuation ⁠briefly surpassed $2tn, its momentum began to lose steam.

Most chipmakers were lower, ‌including Micron and Broadcom, among others. And Nvidia marked its sixth straight session of losses after the chipmaker’s upbeat revenue forecast did little to lift sentiment.

The Wall Street investment bankers that worked on Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering are set to be awarded a record $550m in underwriting fees, according to the official filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

That is more than they made on SpaceX, which set the previous record at $500m.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley will earn the biggest cut, taking over $200m between them.

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Dan Milmo and Aisha Down

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations.

The opening price of $111.50 per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to around $150bn at the current share price.

Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include the Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher and Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.

Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market, though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.

Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes which it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI.

Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist.

In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”.

Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.

Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based fund, said demand for AI hardware and related technology products was pushing up consumer prices around the world.

She said that, alongside the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, this was adding to inflationary pressures around the globe.

“This calls for a tightening of monetary policy in many economies,” she said.

Speaking at the 2026 Apec summit in Shenzhen, Georgieva warned that both factors would push global inflation to 4.7% this year. She added that the rapid rollout of AI was also contributing to stronger than expected economic growth in several countries, despite the headwinds from the Iran war.

Georgieva said that while the energy shock would eventually dissipate, “AI is for ever” – making it a significant driver of world trade, competitiveness, productivity and economic growth.

AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than one-tenth of the world goods trade, a share that is rapidly rising, she said. But some countries were benefiting more from investment than others.

“To put it simply: you snooze, you lose,” she added. “Countries need digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers that are ready for AI, and risk mitigation – especially to control financial stability and cybersecurity risks.”

Lisa Bonos in San Francisco

Sameer Shariff, co-founder and CEO of English language education company Cambly, noticed a buzz of energy among Anthropic employees as they were leaving the company’s headquarters in San Francisco yesterday.

Over the past two years, a few employees have left his company to join Anthropic. He’s been thinking about them today.

“I’m happy for them. It’s a big day for the market and for AI,” Shariff said, while chatting with a friend at Joe and the Juice in downtown San Francisco on Thursday. So far, “Anthropic has been funded by all these investors with the inside scoop. But this is a test of how Wall Street responds … all of a sudden the general public has access to participate.”

Shariff said he’s curious how the next six to 12 months will go. “I’m a big fan,” he added.

As we await the close of market valuation of Anthropic at the end of its first day on the market, Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at US-based Walser Wealth Management, wrote: “Anthropic’s IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment, which has been depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks.”

Walser added: “It’s possible that Anthropic could see volatility and downside moves during the Jensen Huang Senate testimony after Thanksgiving, because that is likely to reignite AI fears.

“But if that happens, it could be a good entry point for investors who want to buy Anthropic.”

Lisa Bonos in San Francisco

On a drizzly morning in downtown San Francisco after a massive storm the day before, the mood was sleepy in the Andytown coffee shop atop Salesforce Tower Park. When asked about Anthropic’s IPO today, one barista said “What’s that?” — a clue that not everyone in this tech hub is obsessed with AI.

Anthropic workers do frequent the coffee shop, but they hadn’t seen any today, her colleague said. One patron, smiled when asked if he worked at the maker of Claude. “No, but I wish I did,” he said.

Out on the street, foot traffic seemed lighter than normal, likely due to the weather. But still some tech workers trickled into their offices at 9:30 a.m.

“I wish I was in that building,” a Meta worker, who declined to give his name, said entering his downtown San Francisco office and gesturing to one of Anthropic’s offices across the street. His friends who work at Anthropic have “big plans for what to do with their newfound wads of cash,” he said. “Some people are planning to backpack Asia,” he said. But mostly, they plan to keep working and liquidate slowly, he added.
